title: Cross-Origin Requests
subtopics: Why a frontend library cannot independently override browser security restrictions
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of cross-origin requests in a jQuery application.
Apply same-origin policy in a small example and describe its expected result.
Verify cors fundamentals with an explicit test or browser observation.
status_note: Draft generated from the attached syllabus and official references; requires lesson-by-lesson technical review, local execution, accessibility checks, and editorial approval.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will work through cross-origin requests with a focused jQuery example. The subtopics below preserve the supplied curriculum coverage and connect the API idea to a small browser interface.
content.why_it_matters: This topic is useful because it turns same-origin policy into a repeatable implementation choice. AJAX sends HTTP requests without requiring a full-page navigation. Treat network errors, HTTP failures, CORS policy, authentication, timeouts, and malformed response data as distinct cases.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a local HTML page with jQuery 4.0.0 loaded before app.js for JavaScript snippets. HTML and package-manager snippets can be checked as configuration examples. Run the interaction in browser DevTools, inspect the DOM/Network panel, and compare actual behavior with the expected result. Do not submit learner code to the production API for arbitrary execution.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original markup and code, clear console/network filters, reload the local page, and repeat the same interaction. For a request example, return the mock endpoint to its original response before retrying.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Start with a known DOM structure, apply the pattern for cross-origin requests, and test one normal case plus one edge case. Keep selectors scoped to the intended component and verify the real browser result.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Implement a request scenario for cross-origin requests against a local or mock endpoint. Demonstrate loading, empty, success, HTTP failure, and network-failure behavior as applicable.

content.task: Implement a request scenario for cross-origin requests against a local or mock endpoint. Demonstrate loading, empty, success, HTTP failure, and network-failure behavior as applicable.
task_acceptance_criteria: The implementation demonstrates cross-origin requests using a current, documented approach.
The learner records the expected and actual behavior and checks at least one edge case.
The example preserves semantic HTML and does not render untrusted data as HTML.
The test setup and any runtime limitation are documented honestly.
hints: First identify which DOM nodes and runtime state are involved in cross-origin requests.
Make one small change, inspect the resulting element or request, and compare it with the expected result.
If the result differs, check the selector, script order, browser console, event target, and relevant API documentation before adding more code.
content.expected_output: The browser permits the cross-origin response only if the API server sends suitable CORS headers. The example domain is intentionally non-routable.
common_mistakes: Assuming a selector matched an element without checking the collection length.
Confusing jQuery collections with native DOM elements or live properties with markup attributes.
Using .html() with untrusted data or assuming client-side validation enforces server rules.
Treating a demo snippet as production-ready without testing failure and accessibility states.
summary: Cross-Origin Requests is one part of the ajax and http communication workflow.
AJAX sends HTTP requests without requiring a full-page navigation. Treat network errors, HTTP failures, CORS policy, authentication, timeouts, and malformed response data as distinct cases.
Use the official API or upgrade guide for version-specific behavior and verify an example locally before relying on it.
